title: Sid Catlett as friend and melodic drummer
summary: Sid Catlett played on one of her record sessions and she admires his melodic, listenable drumming.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: You mentioned that Big Sid Catlett was a good friend of yours.
Yes, he was. He was a good friend of mine.
Did he ever play at your house, too?

Oh, yes, he played at my house. In fact he did one record with me, record session. He did -- I can't remember all of the things. What else did we do on that? We did, "The Song is Ended, But the Melody Lingers On." He was on that session with me. Also, Irving Ashby, the guitarist, second guitarist with Nat King Cole. He was on that particular session. So he was a very good friend of mine and a very marvelous, very marvelous drummer.
I remember when he was here with Louis Armstrong, in 1949.
Which was when I first met him.

Yes, he was a marvelous drummer and he was one of the few drummers that, you know, you could sit -- he didn't care to see how much noise he could make. When I say noise, I don't mean it that way. I don't mean noise, but what I'm saying, whatever he did you could sit and listen to him and could tell what he was playing. He followed a melody. And this is sort of unusual, because most drummers have their own little pattern or their own thing that they're doing, you know. They want to see how many sticks they can use, how many brushes, and how many things they can hit on. But Sid was -- he was just like a guy playing a melodic -- an instrument, you know, that carried a melody. You could follow along what he was doing. Very fine. Very fine.
